en: So how can you use the Bun S3 client?
Well, it starts in index.ts for this tool,
but in there I only parse the input provided
by the user. For that, I'm using parseArgs
provided by Node.js. That of course has
nothing to do with the S3 client. It's just
used here to parse the received input
arguments using that bun.argv property,
which gives us access to all these extra
parameters the user entered here.
So that's just some command parsing and then
a switch statement to call different
functions depending on which command the
user chose. So that's obviously not the
interesting part.
Instead, the interesting part starts in the
backup.ts file, for example.
In there, you can see I have the backup
function
and in there, I do a couple of checks to see
what the user is trying to back up, if it's
a file or a folder, if the recursive option
is set.
But then once I know which files the user
wants to back up,
I call uploadFile, which is another function
provided by me, which expects to get a
client, an S3 client as an input.
Where is this client coming from? Well, that
already is a client received by the backup
function. So it was a parameter there too.
So it's set up in index.ts.
There, before we have that switch statement,
I create that S3 client and createClient is
a function in the config.ts file
where I instantiate a new S3 client. S3
client and despite the name, as mentioned
before, this works with all S3 compatible
storage providers.
Now S3 client is coming from Bun because
again, it's a built-in feature, no extra
dependency needed.
So in this config.ts file, I have some
function to validate whether all the env
vars are set and then I instantiate that
client and return the instantiated client
and I set the access key ID to whatever I
found in the env vars and the same for all
these other settings.
Now, one very important note here, I'm doing
this all explicitly here to show you how you
can configure that client,
but we actually wouldn't have to do that
here because the env var names I chose here
are in line with what Bun expects.
So it will actually look for them
automatically
and we could therefore also create the
client like this
and that would work as well. So passing in
no config at all.
You see, if I now run this command, it works
just as before
because again, we already used the defaults.
I'm just providing this explicit
configuration here for demo purposes.
But that is the main thing that creates this
client and then this client is used in
backup.ts and also in the other files.
In backup.ts, in the uploadFile function,
it's used to Guess what? Upload a file.
To do that, I first get hold of the file
using the Bun file API, so of the local file
which I wanna upload,
and then I use the S3 client and its file
method to get hold of a remote file or
create such a remote file, so a file in that
S3 bucket
with the file method. That method receives a
key, which is in the end the file name and
path on that remote storage.
And that key is a parameter I'm getting
here. So this file method here is coming
from the S3 client and this file handle then
has various methods we can call. For
example, delete to delete the file, exists
to check if that file exists in the remote
storage
or also a
write
method to create the file and fill it with
some content or stat in this case here,
which gives us some statistics, some
information about that file, specifically
the size which I'm using for this basic size
check.
To determine whether something should be
skipped.
If it should not be skipped, I also check
the file size and I have a large file
threshold set up here to 10 megabytes.
And if the file which I'm trying to upload,
which I'm trying to back up is large,
I use a slightly different approach for
uploading that to take advantage of Bun's
built-in multipart uploading feature because
Bun does support uploading both small and
large files to S3 and compatible storage
providers. And for large files, it uses a
process called multipart uploading, which
simply splits those files into smaller
chunks and uploads them chunk by chunk and
gives you a stream to which you can listen
to see the live progress. And that's what
we're setting up here. Again, using the S3
client and that remote file handle,
we create a writer which is an object that
allows us to upload files chunk by chunk
where we define the chunk size of each
individual chunk. So the chunks into which
this big file will be split automatically,
how many parts should be uploaded in
parallel and how often we wanna retry if a
part fails. And then we have this for loop
to go through all these chunks and simply
write them to that remote storage and upload
them to the remote storage chunk by chunk.
That's what we do for large files. For small
files, we don't need that. Instead, we use
that remote file handle and just call write
to just create that remote file and fill it
with the content of the local file.
That is how we upload a file to S3 using
Bun's S3 client.
We can also pass some metadata to write
where we set the type of the file to the
local file type, where we also can set how
often this should be retried and a couple of
other settings.
And indeed, this will also support multipart
uploads out of the box, so you wouldn't even
need this more complex approach, but this
approach gives you more control and allows
you to manually go through chunk by chunk
and for example, add detailed logging. But
even just using this approach would
automatically handle large files as well. I
just have this approach in here for demo
purposes.
So that's how files are uploaded.
